title: settle whether re._cache is saturated at 512 after import (Contested) with a one-line startup probe

headline.statement: The literal claim is TRUE and it means nothing. len(re._cache) == 512 after `import src.app.main` because 512 is the stdlib ceiling and the import chain saturates it on its own - and every single pattern the request path compiles at import time is evicted on the way there.
headline.the_one_line_answer: Yes, it is 512, and the number is a property of CPython rather than of this application: re._MAXCACHE is 512, and 512 distinct patterns fit.
headline.urgency_implied: URGENT rather than optional. re._cache is already full of 512 THIRD-PARTY patterns before the app serves a single request, so it provides zero reuse for the application's own patterns - all 16 of them recompile on first use. The design conclusion (memoize the attack-scan and log-sanitizer patterns at module level) holds either way, as the bead said; what changes is that it is the only cache available.

instrument.why_outside_the_repo: It is an operator probe that must run as its own process: it measures the state of re._cache immediately after an import, so anything else in the process - a test session, conftest, a plugin that imports something - would change the answer. Committed under src/benchmarks/ it would also become importable by a test, and src/AGENTS.md forbids a harness on an import path a test imports.
instrument.counted_before_anything_else_touches_the: len(re._cache) is read immediately after `import src.app.main` and before the residency pass, so no later step can be blamed for the number.
instrument.two_arms: steady: the cache as the interpreter leaves it. purge: re.purge() first. The purge arm exists to separate 'the application uses 512 patterns' from 'the ceiling is full'; it reports how many patterns were already cached before the purge, which is how the two readings are told apart.
instrument.residency_rule: A pattern is resident iff (type(p), p.pattern, p.flags) is still a key of re._cache.
instrument.no_pattern_is_built_by_the_probe: ip_filter._BAD_BOT_REGEX is excluded on purpose: it is built lazily on the first request, and calling its builder here would insert a freshly compiled pattern into the very cache being measured.

protocol.worktree: /home/ansible/pjom, detached, created from a bundle because nothing is pushed
protocol.why_one_arm_per_process: re._cache is process-global, so the two arms must not share an interpreter. The purge arm runs in its own process.
protocol.settings_source: src/.env copied from the target checkout; the probe never opens a DB or Redis connection
protocol.no_windows_number_used: A-5 holds: this is a Linux measurement. The Windows interpreter cannot import the app anyway, because its venv is absent.

steady_arm.what_that_zero_means: Nothing else in the interpreter had compiled a pattern before the app import, so the steady state is not an accumulation carried in from startup: it is produced entirely by the import chain.

purge_arm.what_those_35_mean: The `re` module's own import compiled 35 patterns. After purging them the app import again lands on exactly 512, which is the whole answer: the import chain alone drives the cache to its ceiling.

the_contested_claim.verdict: CONFIRMED as a number, REFUTED as a count. 512 is re._MAXCACHE, so a reading of 512 is a tautology about the ceiling. The 'import-order dependent' half is also wrong in the direction that matters: the saturation is caused by the import itself, not by what happened to run before it.

residency_after_import.how_they_were_chosen: Named explicitly, module by module, from a grep of re.compile across src/: the middleware attack patterns, the log sanitizer, the path sanitizer, the tenant slug patterns, the password validators, the TOTP and backup-code patterns, the cache-key bracket pattern and the request-id pattern. A glob would have produced a denominator nobody chose, and this bead is about a specific set.
residency_after_import.consequence: Each of these is compiled at import, then evicted before the import finishes, so the stdlib cache gives them nothing. The first request that touches one pays the full compile.

what_occupies_the_cache.observation: The entries that displaced the application's patterns are route patterns from billing and checkout libraries, compiled at their own import time - `^/billing/...and `^/checkouts/...` and `^/invoices/...`. The application's patterns lose their slots to a third party that imported later.
what_occupies_the_cache.implication: Nothing in this repository can reclaim those slots at runtime, because eviction is FIFO and the cache is shared process-wide. Only holding the compiled objects in a module global - which the code already does - keeps them.

patterns: src/app/core/env_validator.py:93 - re.match(rules['pattern'], value), a DYNAMIC pattern
compiled_on_first_call_not_at_import.why_they_cannot_be_tested_for_residency: They are not in the cache at import time, so asking whether they survived eviction has no answer.
compiled_on_first_call_not_at_import.why_they_matter_more: Every call re-enters re._compile against a cache that is already at its ceiling, so each such call takes the full compile path and then evicts something else. core/config/auth.py:31-37 runs four such lookups per password validation.

relation_to_the_confirmed_perf_fact.confirmed_fact: Cold 17-branch compile costs 3 917 us (one branch 692 us, three branches 1 133 us) while a warm compile from the module cache costs 5.9 us (perf D13).
relation_to_the_confirmed_perf_fact.what_this_adds: D13 measured the prize: 5.9 us versus 3 917 us is a 663x difference, and it is only reachable if the compiled object is held in a module-level global. This measurement shows the stdlib cache is NOT a route to it - the cache is full before the app serves anything, and all 16 application patterns are evicted. The prize is reachable only through the module global the code already uses.
relation_to_the_confirmed_perf_fact.therefore: The bead's stated conclusion - memoize the attack-scan patterns ourselves rather than relying on re._cache - holds, and it is not merely a good idea: relying on re._cache was never going to work at all.

decision.conclusion: Keep every application pattern as a module-level compiled object. Do not rely on re._cache for any of them.
decision.already_true_for_the_named_16: All 16 are module-level or class-level globals compiled once at import, which is the correct shape. Nothing in this measurement requires a code change.
decision.what_it_does_not_settle: The three inline-literal call sites listed under compiled_on_first_call_not_at_import. Hoisting them to module level is a one-line-each change with a measured prize, but it is not this bead: M-10 is a probe that informs urgency, and the urgency is now established.
decision.no_code_change_made: This bead asked for a measurement, not a change. Nothing under src/ was edited.

measured: len(re._cache) == 512 in both arms, on Linux, at 1feceab21
the purge arm shows 35 patterns cached before the purge, so the app import alone re-saturates to 512
0 of the 16 named request-path patterns are resident after the import
the cache is occupied by third-party billing and checkout route patterns
inferred: FIFO eviction is what displaced them: the stdlib evicts the oldest entry when the cache is full, and the displacers imported after the application did. [Inference] - the observation is which patterns remain; the eviction ORDER is the documented CPython behaviour, not something this probe observed directly.
explicitly_not_measured: The wall-clock cost of the recompiles on the request path. D13's 5.9 us warm figure is quoted from perf, not re-measured here.
Whether any single request actually hits a recompile. That needs a request-path profile, which is what the settled design would be measured against, not this probe.
The pre-3.7 behaviour, and any other interpreter. The ceiling has been 512 since CPython 3.7; the repository's floor is higher, but it was not exercised here.

limits: One interpreter, one commit, one platform: CPython 3.13.16 on Linux at 1feceab21. The saturation is a property of CPython's ceiling plus this import graph; a different interpreter version with a different _MAXCACHE would report a different 512.

The pattern set is the 16 named in the probe, chosen by reading the grep of re.compile across src/. A pattern compiled by a dependency and used on our request path would not appear in the list, and there is no way to enumerate those from inside the process.

Residency is sampled ONCE, immediately after the import. The cache keeps filling as the process runs, so a pattern resident at this instant could be evicted later; 0 of 16 resident here is a statement about import time only.
The probe cannot distinguish 'evicted' from 'never compiled' for a pattern that was compiled lazily. That is why ip_filter._BAD_BOT_REGEX is excluded rather than reported as evicted.
Windows is not represented: A-5 holds and the Windows interpreter cannot import the app.
This artefact does not claim the recompiles are a measurable cost on any endpoint. It claims the stdlib cache cannot be the thing that avoids them, which is a structural fact.
